lessons.title: The map before you begin
lessons.sub: Know the shape of the exam and the difference between Academic and General Training.
lessons.body: The exam has four skills: Listening, Reading, Writing and Speaking. Listening and Reading each have 40 questions. Reading is 60 minutes, Writing is 60 minutes, and Speaking is 11 to 14 minutes. Listening is about 30 minutes; the details of transferring answers depend on the test format.
lessons.example: Academic Task 1: summarise visual information. General Training Task 1: write a letter. Task 2: write an essay.
lessons.action: Choose the type in Settings according to the body you will apply to, not by what is easier. Practice here is shortened and is not a full exam simulation.

lessons.title: Build a correct sentence
lessons.sub: Subject, verb and tense before difficult words.
lessons.body: A clear sentence matters more than a long one full of mistakes. Check subject-verb agreement. Use the past if the event is finished, and the present simple for facts and habits.
lessons.example: The number of students has increased. / Many students have joined.
lessons.action: Write 3 sentences about your work, and turn one into the past and one into the future.

lessons.title: Connect the idea to its meaning
lessons.sub: The difference between although, despite and however.
lessons.body: Although is followed by a full clause. Despite is followed by a noun or an ing verb. However links two opposing ideas and often starts a new sentence. Do not use a linking word just because it looks academic.
lessons.example: Although the fee was high, people enrolled. Despite the high fee, people enrolled. The fee was high. However, demand remained strong.
lessons.action: Write two opposing ideas and join them in each way.

lessons.title: Learn words in context
lessons.sub: Learn collocations instead of translation lists.
lessons.body: Write the word with a natural phrase and an example of your own. Review it after a day, then after several days. Be exact about the difference between cause and correlation, and between tentative and certain.
lessons.example: conduct research / make a decision / compelling evidence / a gradual decline
lessons.action: Use 3 phrases in a short paragraph and check the meaning sounds natural.

lessons.title: Read for the idea
lessons.sub: Skimming before details.
lessons.body: Start with the title and the start and end of each paragraph. Decide its topic and function: a problem? an experiment? an objection? Then read the question and go back to where the evidence is. The aim is not to translate every word.
lessons.example: A paragraph describes a pilot, its benefits and two limitations. A suitable heading should cover the whole paragraph, not one detail.
lessons.action: Summarise each paragraph of a reading practice text in one line in English.

lessons.title: Find the evidence
lessons.sub: Scanning for names, dates and numbers.
lessons.body: Mark the question words and their likely synonyms. Find where they are, then read the whole sentence and what surrounds it. The right number may be there but tied to something else.
lessons.example: Question: How long is the loan? Text: Eight books for three weeks. Answer: three weeks, not eight.
lessons.action: Check every answer and mark the sentence that proves it.

lessons.title: True / False / Not Given
lessons.sub: The difference between a negative and missing information
lessons.body: True: the text supports the same meaning. False: the text contradicts it. Not Given: the text is not enough to judge. Do not rely on general knowledge. Watch for all, always and only.
lessons.example: Text: Some learners attended online. Claim: Every learner attended online. You cannot establish every learner from some alone.
lessons.action: Do the garden questions. Before you choose Not Given ask yourself: is there evidence for it or against it?

lessons.title: Understand the writer's caution
lessons.sub: Conclude only as far as the evidence goes.
lessons.body: Tell apart an experiment that proves a cause from a study that notices a relationship. Words like may, suggest and could show the limits of the conclusion. Heading questions must cover the main point, not a small example.
lessons.example: A non-random comparison may show an association; it does not, by itself, establish causation.
lessons.action: Summarise the limits of the roof study or the working week study in one sentence.

lessons.title: Predict before you listen
lessons.sub: Read the question and decide the answer type.
lessons.body: Is a day, number, place or reason needed? Predict the type of information, not the answer itself. While listening focus on context and correction. The practice voice here is generated by the browser, not an official IELTS recording.
lessons.example: A class at six... actually, six thirty. The final time is 6:30.
lessons.action: Listen to the course dialogue without the transcript, and after checking listen again with the transcript.

lessons.title: Watch for the correction
lessons.sub: The answer is not the first number you hear.
lessons.body: The speaker may change the date or the plan. Watch for words like but, instead, actually and now. Tell meeting time apart from departure time, and student price from adult price.
lessons.example: Meet at nine. The bus leaves at nine fifteen. Departure: 9:15.
lessons.action: Write the first piece of information and the correction in the trip dialogue.

lessons.title: Note only what matters
lessons.sub: Short forms instead of writing everything.
lessons.body: Write keywords and numbers. In the official exam follow the word limit and spelling instructions. The choice exercises here do not measure spelling or short-answer writing skill.
lessons.example: secure bike parking → main reason; showers → some; money → few
lessons.action: Summarise the bike lecture in 3 points without the text.

lessons.title: Academic Task 1
lessons.sub: Overview and comparisons.
lessons.body: Start by rephrasing the task. Write an overview of the two main trends, then compare the numbers in groups. Do not invent reasons that are not there. Minimum 150 words; spend about 20 minutes.
lessons.example: The proportion rose from 20% to 30%, an increase of 10 percentage points. This is not the same as a 10% relative increase.
lessons.action: Open the table task in the Writing studio. Pick the highest and lowest values before you start.

lessons.title: General Training Task 1
lessons.sub: A letter in the right style.
lessons.body: Identify the recipient and the purpose. Cover every point in the question and separate them into paragraphs. The style for a friend is different from the style for an official. Minimum 150 words; spend about 20 minutes.
lessons.example: Dear Sir or Madam, I am writing to request... / Dear Sam, Thanks for your message...
lessons.action: Write a formal opening and a friendly opening for the same purpose.

lessons.title: Task 2: build an argument
lessons.sub: A clear position and a developed idea.
lessons.body: Read every part of the question. Plan an introduction, body paragraphs and a conclusion. Each paragraph: an idea, an explanation and a relevant example. Write at least 250 words in about 40 minutes. Task 2 carries more weight than Task 1.
lessons.example: Claim: Libraries should remain funded. Explanation: They provide access to resources. Example: A learner without home internet can use library computers.
lessons.action: Pick a topic in the Writing studio. Plan for 5 minutes, then write and check within the task time.

lessons.title: Speaking: talk, do not memorise
lessons.sub: A natural answer with a reason and an example.
lessons.body: Part 1 asks about you and familiar topics. Part 2 is a cue card, one minute to prepare and up to two minutes of talk. Part 3 is a wider and deeper discussion. Clear pronunciation matters more than copying an accent.
lessons.example: I enjoy teaching because it lets me explain difficult ideas. For example, I recently used a simple experiment to teach...
lessons.action: Record a one-minute answer, listen to it, and note repeated words and long pauses.

lessons.title: Check against clear criteria
lessons.sub: Marking is not about the number of difficult words.
lessons.body: Writing: task achievement/response, coherence and cohesion, lexical resource, grammatical range and accuracy. Speaking: fluency and coherence, vocabulary, grammar, pronunciation. Marking here is self-review, not an official band or automatic score.
lessons.example: After recording: Did I answer the exact question? Did I explain why? Could a listener follow my ideas?
lessons.action: Ask a qualified teacher to review a writing sample and a recording before you decide you are ready for the exam.

lessons.title: Matching headings
lessons.sub: Match the heading to the idea of the whole paragraph.
lessons.body: A heading must sum up the whole paragraph, not one sentence in it. Read the first and last sentence and name the paragraph's idea in two words. Then cross out headings you have already used. Watch for headings that use words from the text but mean something wrong.
lessons.example: Paragraph: "Sleep specialists recommend planning revision earlier and protecting a full night of sleep." Heading: Advice for protecting study time and sleep.
lessons.action: Take a paragraph from any text and write your own heading before you read the options.

lessons.title: Sentence and summary completion
lessons.sub: The word must come from the text and fit the sentence grammatically.
lessons.body: Read the word limit (ONE WORD / TWO WORDS). Decide the type of the missing word: noun? verb? adjective? Look in the text for synonyms of the sentence, and copy the word exactly, with the same spelling. An answer that breaks the limit is wrong even if the meaning is right.
lessons.example: Question: "Energy remains the largest single ___." Text: "energy remains the largest single cost". Answer: cost.
lessons.action: Do a gap-fill exercise and check the word count and spelling.

lessons.title: Multiple choice: common traps
lessons.sub: Choose on evidence, not on feeling.
lessons.body: Wrong options often use words from the text but change the meaning, or overgeneralise (always, all, never), or mix up two opinions. Cross out options until one is left that a sentence in the text supports.
lessons.example: Option: "Reflective roofs always reduce energy use." Text: "may increase winter heating demand". The word always makes it wrong.
lessons.action: Answer 5 questions and write beside each answer the sentence that proves it.

lessons.title: Yes / No / Not Given
lessons.sub: The writer's opinion, not the facts.
lessons.body: In Yes/No/Not Given the question is about the writer's opinion or claim. Yes means the writer agrees, No means the writer disagrees, Not Given means the writer did not say. Never use outside knowledge, even if you are a biology teacher and know the answer.
lessons.example: Writer: "Dismissing concerns works worse than listening." Statement: "Dismissing concerns is effective." Answer: No.
lessons.action: Find the writer's position in the text through words like argue, claim, suggest.

lessons.title: Matching information
lessons.sub: Look for the meaning, not the word.
lessons.body: The question describes a piece of information (an example, a warning or a reason). Look in each paragraph for the idea in different words. The same paragraph can come up again if the instructions allow it. Start with the questions that have numbers or names because they are easier.
lessons.example: Question: "a warning about the reliability of the counts". Text: "counts depend on how much effort is spent searching". Paragraph D.
lessons.action: Write each paragraph's function in one line before you start the questions.

lessons.title: Listening: forms and numbers
lessons.sub: Names, numbers, dates and corrections.
lessons.body: In forms, write the correct spelling. Names are spelled letter by letter. Numbers: thirteen/thirty and fifteen/fifty sound different. Watch out: speakers often correct themselves (Tuesday... actually Wednesday). The answer is the final correction.
lessons.example: "It runs on Tuesday mornings. Actually, it is now on Wednesday." Answer: Wednesday.
lessons.action: Listen to the first clip of the test and note every correction you hear.

lessons.title: Listening: multiple choice
lessons.sub: The answer is said with a different meaning.
lessons.body: Questions follow the order of the speech. Read the options and know the differences between them before the audio. The answer is rarely said in the option's own words, and the wrong option is often mentioned too and then rejected.
lessons.example: Option B: "It would show clearer differences" ← "a nature reserve would show clearer differences".
lessons.action: Write two synonyms for each option before you listen.

lessons.title: Listening Section 4: the lecture
lessons.sub: One lecture, with no break.
lessons.body: Section 4 is an academic lecture with one voice. Follow the structure: introduction, main points, examples. Answers are usually one word from the lecture, so write what you hear with correct spelling. Get used to scientific terms by reading biology and environment vocabulary.
lessons.example: Lecture: "enzyme helps luciferin react with oxygen". Gap: molecule called ___. Answer: luciferin.
lessons.action: Listen to Section 4, take handwritten notes, then compare.

lessons.title: Listening: predicting and synonyms
lessons.sub: The synonym matters more than the matching word.
lessons.body: The question says safety glasses and the speaker says eye protection. Train yourself to hear the meaning. Write likely synonyms while you read the question, before the recording.
lessons.example: Question: "Bring your own coat". Speaker: "we can lend you glasses but not a coat".
lessons.action: Pick 5 questions and write synonyms for each one.

lessons.title: Task 1: tables and charts
lessons.sub: Overview first, then selected numbers.
lessons.body: Write 4 paragraphs: an introduction that rephrases the question, an overview with the two main trends and no numbers, one detail paragraph with selected numbers, and a second detail paragraph. Compare, do not copy every number. Do not explain causes because you do not know them.
lessons.example: Overall, car use fell while bus and bicycle use rose. In 2010, 60% of commuters drove, compared with 45% in 2025.
lessons.action: Write only the overview paragraph for one Task 1 and review it.

lessons.title: Task 1: the process
lessons.sub: The passive and sequence words.
lessons.body: Describe the stages in order using the passive: is pumped, are added. Use First, Next, After that, Finally. State the number of stages in the overview. Do not add stages that are not in the diagram.
lessons.example: The process has six stages. First, water is pumped from a river into a storage tank.
lessons.action: Write 3 passive sentences from the process.

lessons.title: Task 2: essay structure
lessons.sub: A position, two body paragraphs and a conclusion.
lessons.body: Analyse the question: discuss both views? agree? problem and solution? Each type has its own structure. Introduction: background and your position. Body paragraph: main idea, explanation, example. Conclusion: summarise with no new ideas. Plan for 5 minutes before you write.
lessons.example: Thesis: "In my view, GM crops can help, provided they are tested carefully."
lessons.action: Plan a Task 2 essay in 5 minutes without writing it.

lessons.title: Cohesion and variety
lessons.sub: Use linking words wisely, not often.
lessons.body: Use However, In addition and For example in the right places. Do not start every sentence with a linking word. Mix simple and complex sentences. Use pronouns (this, these) to refer back to an earlier sentence. Replace repeated words with precise synonyms.
lessons.example: Sleep improves memory. This effect is strongest for facts, whereas skills benefit from lighter sleep.
lessons.action: Check your last draft and cross out repeated words.

lessons.title: Scientific caution: hedging
lessons.sub: may, suggest, tend to.
lessons.body: In scientific writing avoid generalising. Use may, could, tends to, the evidence suggests. This makes the language more precise and fits the scientific texts you read.
lessons.example: "The data suggest a possible link" Replace "This proves".
lessons.action: Turn 3 absolute sentences into cautious ones.

lessons.title: Complex sentences with accuracy
lessons.sub: Relative clauses and conditionals.
lessons.body: Use relative clauses (who, which, that) to add information. Second conditional: If + past, would + infinitive. One correct complex sentence is better than three complex sentences with errors.
lessons.example: Farmers who use drought-tolerant crops may lose less in a dry year.
lessons.action: Write 3 sentences with a relative clause.

lessons.title: Paraphrasing
lessons.sub: Synonyms and changing structure.
lessons.body: Change the words (increase → rise) and the structure (active → passive). Keep the meaning. Use this in the Task 1 and Task 2 introductions and when you understand questions.
lessons.example: "The number of visitors rose" → "There was an increase in visitor numbers".
lessons.action: Rephrase 5 sentences from a reading text.

lessons.title: Speaking Part 2
lessons.sub: One minute to prepare, then continuous speech.
lessons.body: Use the minute to write keywords for the four points. Start with an introduction, follow the points, and add a reason and a feeling. If you have nothing, invent a believable example. Speaking continuously for two minutes matters more than difficult words.
lessons.example: Cue: Describe a teacher... Start: "I would like to talk about my biology teacher, Mr ...".
lessons.action: Record a whole Part 2 and listen back.

lessons.title: Speaking Part 3
lessons.sub: Opinion, reason, comparison.
lessons.body: Part 3 asks abstract questions. Use the pattern: my opinion + reason + example + contrast. Use I would say, it depends on, to some extent. Do not rely on memorised answers.
lessons.example: "It depends on the age. For young children, small groups may work better because..."
lessons.action: Answer 4 Part 3 questions in two minutes.

lessons.title: Time management in the test
lessons.sub: 20 minutes per text, and do not fall behind.
lessons.body: In Reading split the sixty minutes: about 20 for each text, and keep the last 5 minutes to check. If a question is hard, mark it and move on. In Listening read the next section's questions during the break. In Writing: 20 minutes for Task 1 and 40 for Task 2.
lessons.example: Plan: Passage 1 (0–18), Passage 2 (18–38), Passage 3 (38–58), check (58–60).
lessons.action: Try a 20-minute timer on one text.

lessons.title: Science and environment vocabulary
lessons.sub: Words that repeat in Reading and Listening.
lessons.body: Biology, environment and medicine topics are common in Academic. Learn words like habitat, species, evidence, hypothesis. Understand them in sentences and with synonyms. The cards in the Words section repeat them for you with a Leitner system.
lessons.example: The study found a significant correlation, but correlation does not prove cause.
lessons.action: Review 10 cards from the Words section.

reading.title: Bees in the city
paras: A

For many years, scientists assumed that wild bees did best in the countryside, where flowers are plentiful and pesticides are, in theory, easier to avoid. A recent survey of twelve European cities challenged that view. Researchers counted wild bee species in city parks, on rooftops and along railway lines, then compared the results with counts from nearby farmland. In several cities, the urban sites supported at least as many species as the farmland.
B

The explanation lies in the variety of habitat found in a city. Gardens, allotments and parks flower at different times of the year, so food is available from early spring until late autumn. Farmland, by contrast, often produces a single crop that blossoms for only a few weeks. Cities also tend to be warmer than the surrounding countryside, which allows some species to become active earlier in the year.
C

Nesting is another important factor. Most wild bees do not live in hives. About seventy per cent nest in bare soil, and the rest use hollow stems, dead wood or gaps in walls. Tidy lawns and sealed pavements remove nesting sites for ground-nesting species, but cities often contain neglected corners, such as railway embankments and abandoned plots, that are left undisturbed for years. One research team found that a single strip of rough ground beside a railway line held more nests than an entire manicured park of the same size.
D

However, the picture is not entirely positive. The survey also showed that the species found in cities were not the same as those in the countryside. Cities favoured small, adaptable bees that can feed on many kinds of flower, while larger specialists that depend on one particular plant were rare. A city with many species can therefore still be missing the ones that conservationists worry about most. In addition, the researchers noted that counts depend on how much effort is spent searching, and that some cities had been surveyed more thoroughly than others.
E

Planners are already acting on the findings. In one city, the council now delays the mowing of road verges until late summer, and in another, new buildings must include a green roof planted with a mixture of flowering species. Volunteers have built "bee hotels" from drilled wood blocks, although the survey team cautioned that these mainly benefit a few common species and may spread disease if they are not cleaned regularly. The researchers' advice is simple: leave some soil bare, let some plants flower, and resist the urge to tidy everything.

reading.title: Sleeping on it
paras: A

Many students believe that an all-night revision session is the best way to prepare for an exam. Sleep researchers disagree. Over the past few decades, laboratory studies have suggested that sleep is not simply a rest for the body. It appears to be an active period during which the brain organises what has been learned during the day.
B

In a typical experiment, volunteers learn a list of word pairs in the evening. Half of them sleep normally, while the others stay awake all night. Both groups then sleep normally for two further nights, so that simple tiredness does not affect the results, and are tested on the word pairs. The group that slept on the first night usually remembers more pairs.
C

Scientists think the explanation involves a process called consolidation. During deep sleep, patterns of brain activity that occurred during learning seem to be replayed, which may strengthen the connections between the cells involved. Memories for facts and events appear to benefit most from deep sleep, while physical skills, such as playing a piece of music, seem to benefit more from the lighter stages of sleep that occur late in the night.
D

Timing may also matter. In a small trial involving sixty secondary school pupils, one group reviewed new vocabulary shortly before going to bed and another group reviewed it the next morning. Both groups were tested the following day. The first group scored slightly higher, but the difference had almost disappeared a week later. The researchers pointed out that the pupils had not been assigned to the groups at random, so factors such as motivation could have influenced the result.
E

Sleep specialists do not claim that studying the night before an exam is pointless. Instead, they recommend planning revision earlier in the week and protecting a full night of sleep before the test. Caffeine late in the afternoon can delay sleep, and some studies suggest that bright screens in the hour before bed have the same effect, although the evidence is still developing. A short nap of up to twenty minutes can improve alertness, but its benefits for memory are less clear.
F

There are limits to what the research can show. Most laboratory studies use simple material such as word lists, so it is uncertain how far the findings apply to complex subjects such as genetics or organic chemistry. In addition, people differ in how much sleep they need, and a rule of eight hours may not suit everybody. Nevertheless, the broad message is consistent: learning does not end when the book is closed.

reading.title: Fresh water from the sea
paras: A

Hundreds of millions of people live in regions where fresh water is scarce, and the problem is growing as populations rise and rainfall patterns change. One response is desalination, the removal of salt from seawater. The idea is not new: sailors boiled seawater to produce drinking water centuries ago. What has changed is the scale. Today, thousands of plants supply cities, industries and farms, particularly in dry coastal countries.
B

Most modern plants use reverse osmosis. Seawater is forced at high pressure through a membrane that allows water molecules to pass but blocks most of the dissolved salt. The process is far more efficient than older methods that relied on heating the water, and the energy needed to produce a cubic metre of fresh water has fallen by roughly half over the past thirty years. Even so, energy remains the largest single cost, often accounting for a third to a half of the price of the water.
C

Environmental concerns centre on the concentrated salty water left over, known as brine. If it is released carelessly, it can sink to the seabed and reduce oxygen levels, harming organisms that cannot move away. Engineers have responded by installing long pipes that spread the brine over a wide area and dilute it quickly. Some plants now go further and extract valuable minerals such as magnesium from the brine, although this is not yet profitable everywhere.
D

Critics argue that desalination encourages complacency. If water seems unlimited, they say, there is less pressure to repair leaking pipes, which in some cities waste a quarter or more of the supply, or to persuade households to use less. Supporters reply that the technology is only one part of a broader strategy. In one dry region, for example, authorities combine desalinated water with recycled wastewater and strict limits on garden irrigation.
E

Cost is the other major issue. Desalinated water is typically more expensive than water from rivers or wells, which makes it difficult for poorer countries to adopt. Falling membrane prices and the use of solar power are narrowing the gap, and small solar-powered units have been installed in remote island communities. However, a plant that relies on solar panels alone cannot operate at night unless it stores energy, and storage adds to the cost.
F

Most experts conclude that desalination will be a necessary tool but not a universal solution. Where seawater is nearby and energy is affordable, it can protect a city against drought. Inland regions face a harder problem, because transporting water uphill over long distances uses so much energy that other measures are usually cheaper.

reading.title: Coral reefs under pressure
paras: A

Coral reefs cover less than one per cent of the ocean floor, yet they are home to around a quarter of all marine species. Reef-building corals are animals that live in partnership with microscopic algae. The algae live inside the coral's tissue, supply it with most of its food through photosynthesis, and give it its colour.
B

When the water becomes too warm, this partnership breaks down. The coral expels the algae and turns pale, an event known as bleaching. A bleached coral is not dead, but it is starving and more vulnerable to disease. If temperatures return to normal within a few weeks, many colonies can recover. If the heat lasts, they die.
C

Large bleaching events have become more frequent in recent decades. In some regions, surveys show that reefs now face a major event about every six years, which leaves too little time for slow-growing corals to regrow between events. Scientists warn that the gaps between events are likely to shrink further if the oceans continue to warm.
D

Not all corals respond in the same way. Branching species grow quickly but are fragile, whereas massive, boulder-shaped species grow slowly and tend to survive heat better. In one regional survey, reefs made mostly of boulder-shaped corals lost fewer colonies than reefs dominated by branching types. Some corals also host heat-tolerant algae, which may allow them to survive higher temperatures.
E

There are reasons for cautious hope. Laboratories are breeding colonies selected for heat tolerance, and some of these have been transplanted to damaged reefs. Local action matters too. Reducing pollution and overfishing gives reefs a better chance of recovering, because healthy reefs with plenty of grazing fish recover faster: the fish eat the seaweed that would otherwise smother young coral.
F

None of these measures can replace cuts in greenhouse gas emissions. Restoration projects work at a small scale, usually a few hectares, while reef systems stretch for thousands of kilometres. Most researchers therefore treat restoration as a way of buying time and protecting the most valuable sites, not as a cure.

reading.title: A short history of vaccination
paras: A

Long before vaccines existed, people noticed that survivors of some diseases rarely caught them twice. In several parts of Asia and Africa, healers practised variolation: they scratched material from a smallpox sore into the skin of a healthy person, hoping to cause a mild illness that would protect against a severe one. It worked often enough to spread, but a small proportion of patients died from the procedure itself.
B

In 1796 the English doctor Edward Jenner tested a safer idea. He had heard that dairy workers who caught cowpox, a mild disease of cattle, seemed to be protected from smallpox. He inoculated a boy with material from a cowpox sore and later exposed him to smallpox; the boy did not become ill. By today's standards the experiment would be considered unethical, but it led to the first widely used vaccine. The word "vaccine" itself comes from the Latin word for cow.
C

For another century, nobody knew why vaccination worked. In the 1880s, Louis Pasteur showed that weakened forms of a germ could protect animals from the full disease, and his team developed a vaccine against rabies. Over the following decades, scientists learned to identify the specific germs that cause diseases and to grow them in the laboratory, which made large-scale production possible.
D

Vaccination campaigns have had dramatic results. In 1980 the World Health Organization declared that smallpox had been eradicated, the only human disease so far to have been removed completely. Polio has been eliminated from most countries, and measles deaths have fallen sharply, although the disease returns whenever vaccination rates drop. High coverage matters because it also protects people who cannot be vaccinated, an effect known as community protection.
E

New technologies are changing how vaccines are made. Traditional vaccines use weakened or inactivated germs. Newer types deliver only the genetic instructions for making a harmless piece of the germ, which the body's cells then produce, training the immune system to recognise it. This approach allows developers to design a candidate vaccine within days of identifying a new threat, although testing for safety and effectiveness still takes months.
F

Even so, vaccines face a challenge of public trust. Surveys in many countries show that most parents support routine immunisation, but a vocal minority are hesitant, often because of rumours spread online. Health workers say that listening to specific worries, and explaining both the benefits and the rare side effects honestly, works better than dismissing concerns.

reading.title: Growing food upwards
paras: A

A vertical farm grows crops in stacked layers inside a building, usually under LED lighting and without soil. The roots are supplied with water containing dissolved nutrients, a method called hydroponics, and sensors adjust temperature, humidity and light for each variety. Because everything is controlled, a farm can harvest lettuce and herbs all year round, whatever the weather outside.
B

Supporters point to several advantages. Vertical farms can use up to ninety per cent less water than field farming because the water is recycled, and they often need no pesticides because pests are kept out of sealed rooms. They can be built close to cities, which shortens the distance that fresh produce must travel and so reduces spoilage. In land-scarce countries with harsh climates, they offer a way to grow some food locally.
C

The difficulty is cost. Lighting and cooling use large amounts of electricity, and the buildings are expensive to equip. As a result, vertical farms have so far concentrated on high-value crops such as leafy greens, herbs and strawberries. Staple crops such as wheat and rice, which provide most of the world's calories, need much more light and space for each kilogram produced, and growing them indoors is not currently economical.
D

Several start-up companies have closed after failing to cover their energy bills, and critics argue that early optimism was exaggerated. Defenders reply that the industry is young. LED efficiency continues to improve, and some farms now buy electricity from wind and solar sources. One company in a cold northern country has even built its farm beside a factory and uses the factory's waste heat to warm the building.
E

Researchers also see vertical farms as laboratories. Because conditions can be controlled precisely, plant scientists can test how a single factor, such as the colour of the light, changes the growth or flavour of a crop without interference from the weather. Findings from this work may eventually benefit ordinary greenhouses, which are cheaper to run.
F

For the foreseeable future, therefore, vertical farming looks likely to complement rather than replace conventional agriculture. It may be most valuable where land or fresh water is limited, and where consumers will pay slightly more for locally grown produce.

listening.title: Lecture: living light
listening.ctx: A lecturer talks about bioluminescence, the production of light by living things.
script: Today I would like to talk about bioluminescence, the production of light by living organisms. It occurs in fireflies, fungi, bacteria and a very large number of sea animals.

The basic chemistry is the same in most cases. An enzyme helps a molecule called luciferin to react with oxygen, and the reaction releases energy as light rather than as heat. This is why the light is often called cold light.
The scientific interest goes back a long way. In the seventeenth century, Robert Boyle showed that the glow of rotting wood needed air. Remove the air, and the light disappeared.

Why do animals make light? Fireflies flash in patterns that are specific to each species, and this allows the right partners to find each other. In the deep sea, the anglerfish has a glowing lure that attracts smaller fish close enough to catch. Other animals use light for defence. Some shrimp produce light on their undersides to match the faint blue light coming from above, so that predators looking up cannot see their outline. This is called counter-illumination.

Water also has an effect on the colour. Blue light travels furthest in sea water, so most light in the deep ocean is blue. Some microscopic organisms called dinoflagellates glow when the water is disturbed, which is why a boat can leave a glowing trail at night.
Glowing has a cost, however. A light signal can reveal an animal's position to predators, so many species can switch it on and off or hide it.

Finally, research in medicine. The gene that produces the glowing enzyme is used as a marker, so that scientists can track cells in a living animal. In another project, researchers have designed bacteria that glow when they detect arsenic in drinking water, which could make testing cheap and simple in remote villages.

listening.title: Lecture: how sea turtles navigate
listening.ctx: A marine biology lecturer discusses how sea turtles find their way.
script: Today I will talk about navigation in sea turtles. A female loggerhead turtle can swim thousands of kilometres across the ocean, and then return to nest on the same stretch of beach where she herself hatched. How does she do it?

The first clue came from experiments in the nineteen nineties. Researchers placed young turtles in a large tank surrounded by coils that produced different magnetic fields. The turtles changed direction when the field changed, which showed they can sense the magnetic field of the Earth.

The Earth's field varies in two ways: its strength, and the angle at which its lines meet the surface. Each coastal region has a slightly different combination. The leading idea is that turtles learn the magnetic signature of their home beach as hatchlings, and look for it again as adults. This is called magnetic imprinting.

Magnetism is not the only cue. Close to the shore, turtles use smell, and they also respond to wave direction. Hatchlings find the sea by moving towards the brightest horizon, which is normally over the water.

This causes a modern problem: artificial lights. On beaches with street lights or hotels, hatchlings can crawl towards the buildings instead of the sea. Many conservation groups now ask hotels to use dim, amber lighting, which is less attractive to turtles.

Another concern is that the magnetic signature of a beach slowly changes over decades. Some scientists suggest that this may explain why nesting sites shift. There is still disagreement, and more data from tagged turtles is needed.
To finish, here is a surprising number. Only about one in a thousand hatchlings survives to adulthood, so every nest that is protected matters.

While supporters see them as a practical solution, critics worry about unknown risks. In my view, GM crops can help, provided they are tested carefully and regulated.

Those in favour point first to yield and resilience. Some GM varieties resist pests or tolerate drought, which can protect harvests in regions where farmers have few alternatives. For example, a drought-tolerant maize variety may allow a family to keep growing food in a dry year. In addition, crops that need fewer pesticides could reduce costs and chemical pollution.

On the other hand, opponents raise legitimate concerns. Some fear that modified genes could spread to wild plants, and others worry that a few companies would control the seed supply, making small farmers dependent on them. These risks are not imaginary, but they relate mainly to regulation and ownership rather than to the technology itself.

In my opinion, the evidence so far suggests that approved GM crops are safe to eat, so a complete ban would be unjustified. The clearing of forests, wetlands and grasslands for homes and farms is accelerating in many countries. This causes serious ecological and social problems, but there are practical ways to reduce the damage.

The most direct problem is the loss of biodiversity. When a habitat is destroyed, the animals and plants that depend on it may disappear locally, and some species have nowhere else to live. A second problem is the loss of services that nature provides for free. Wetlands, for instance, absorb floodwater, so building on them can increase flood damage for nearby communities.

Several measures could address this. First, governments can protect the most valuable areas by law and enforce penalties for illegal clearing. Second, cities can build upwards rather than outwards, using existing land more densely so that fewer new sites are needed. Farmers can also be given incentives to leave strips of natural vegetation along fields, which keeps wildlife corridors open at little cost.

vocab.def: a statement or idea that can be tested by an experiment
vocab.ex: The experiment was designed to test the hypothesis.

vocab.def: a factor that can change or be changed in an experiment
vocab.ex: Only one variable was changed in the test.

vocab.def: facts or signs that show whether something is true
vocab.ex: There is little evidence that the method works.

vocab.def: large or important enough to notice; (statistics) unlikely to be chance
vocab.ex: There was a significant increase in yield.

vocab.def: a small group taken from a larger one to be studied
vocab.ex: A small sample may not represent everyone.

vocab.def: always acting or happening in the same way; in agreement with
vocab.ex: The results were consistent with earlier studies.

vocab.def: to help cause something to happen
vocab.ex: Pollution contributes to respiratory disease.

vocab.def: one of the things that influences a result
vocab.ex: Diet is only one factor in good health.

vocab.def: to come from a source
vocab.ex: Many drugs derive from plants.

vocab.def: to come into view or become known
vocab.ex: A clear pattern emerged from the data.

vocab.def: able to be trusted to give the same result
vocab.ex: A reliable result can be repeated.

vocab.def: an unfair leaning towards or against something
vocab.ex: Random selection reduces bias.

vocab.def: a link between two things that change together
vocab.ex: A correlation does not prove a cause.

vocab.def: to make something less severe or harmful
vocab.ex: Trees can mitigate the heat in cities.

vocab.def: large in amount or importance
vocab.ex: A substantial amount of water is wasted.

vocab.def: to fall in number or quality; a fall
vocab.ex: The population of the species declined.

vocab.def: to go up and down in an irregular way
vocab.ex: Temperatures fluctuated during the week.

vocab.def: the highest point; to reach the highest point
vocab.ex: Sales peaked in July.

vocab.def: to stay the same without big changes
vocab.ex: The figure remained stable at 20%.

vocab.def: to make up a part of a total
vocab.ex: Energy accounts for half of the cost.

vocab.def: able to continue without using up resources or harming the environment
vocab.ex: Sustainable farming protects soil.

vocab.def: the natural home of a plant or animal
vocab.ex: Wetlands are a habitat for many birds.

vocab.def: a group of living things that can breed together
vocab.ex: Several species are close to extinction.

vocab.def: a community of living things and their environment
vocab.ex: A pond is a small ecosystem.

vocab.def: the variety of living things in an area
vocab.ex: Biodiversity is higher in undisturbed forests.

vocab.def: to change in order to survive in new conditions
vocab.ex: Plants adapt to dry conditions.

vocab.def: any living thing, such as a plant, animal or bacterium
vocab.ex: Microscopic organisms live in the soil.

vocab.def: a change in the DNA of a living thing
vocab.ex: A mutation can change a protein.

vocab.def: the ability to withstand something, such as a drug or disease
vocab.ex: Bacteria can develop resistance to drugs.

vocab.def: the body's system that fights infection
vocab.ex: Vaccines train the immune system.

vocab.def: a substance that living things need to grow
vocab.ex: Roots absorb nutrients from the soil.

vocab.def: the process plants use to turn light, water and carbon dioxide into food
vocab.ex: Photosynthesis needs light and water.

vocab.def: the process cells use to release energy from food
vocab.ex: Cells release energy by respiration.

vocab.def: a unit of heredity that carries instructions for a feature
vocab.ex: A gene carries instructions for a protein.

vocab.def: a protein that speeds up a chemical reaction
vocab.ex: An enzyme speeds up a reaction.

vocab.def: the amount of a substance in a given space or volume
vocab.ex: A high salt concentration slows growth.

vocab.def: something that could cause harm or danger
vocab.ex: Chemicals can be a hazard in the laboratory.

vocab.def: action taken in advance to prevent harm
vocab.ex: Wear gloves as a precaution.

vocab.def: exact and correct in detail
vocab.ex: An accurate scale gives exact masses.

vocab.def: a rough calculation; to calculate roughly
vocab.ex: Experts estimate that numbers will double.

vocab.def: the general direction in which something is changing
vocab.ex: The long-term trend is upward.

vocab.def: a part of a whole, often given as a percentage
vocab.ex: A large proportion of students agreed.

vocab.def: about, not exactly
vocab.ex: Approximately half the seeds germinated.

vocab.def: used to compare two things: while, but
vocab.ex: Cars are popular, whereas bicycles are rare.

vocab.def: in spite of
vocab.ex: Despite the cost, the scheme was approved.

vocab.def: because of this; as a result
vocab.ex: Consequently, fewer plants survived.

vocab.def: but, in contrast to what was just said
vocab.ex: The trial was small. Nevertheless, it was useful.

vocab.def: in addition to what was just said
vocab.ex: Furthermore, the method is cheap.

vocab.def: not certain; made without full confidence
vocab.ex: The findings are tentative.

vocab.def: something accepted as true without proof
vocab.ex: The model rests on a simple assumption.

vocab.def: a likely effect or result of something
vocab.ex: The study has implications for farming.

vocab.def: able to work in practice; workable
vocab.ex: Solar power is a viable option here.

vocab.def: in short supply; hard to find
vocab.ex: Fresh water is scarce in dry regions.

vocab.def: to make a liquid weaker by adding water
vocab.ex: Dilute the acid with water.

vocab.def: to keep safe from loss or damage
vocab.ex: We must conserve energy.

vocab.def: the release of gas or other substances into the air
vocab.ex: Emissions from vehicles have fallen.

vocab.def: able to be replaced naturally, such as wind or solar energy
vocab.ex: Wind is a renewable source of energy.

vocab.def: relating to towns and cities
vocab.ex: Urban areas are warmer than rural ones.

vocab.def: a person or animal that lives in a particular place
vocab.ex: The town has 5,000 inhabitants.

vocab.def: to move from one region to another, usually with the seasons
vocab.ex: Many birds migrate south in winter.

vocab.def: no longer existing, as a species
vocab.ex: The species became extinct.

vocab.def: to be a danger to something
vocab.ex: Pollution threatens fish populations.

vocab.def: to control something by rules or by a system
vocab.ex: Governments regulate pesticide use.

vocab.def: to gain or get something, such as a skill or knowledge
vocab.ex: Children acquire language quickly.

vocab.def: to keep or continue to have
vocab.ex: Students retain more when they practise.

vocab.def: to understand fully
vocab.ex: It is hard to comprehend such large numbers.

vocab.def: the result or effect of an action or process
vocab.ex: The outcome of the trial was positive.

vocab.def: to take on a task or responsibility
vocab.ex: The team undertook a three-year study.
